blocks.text: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department drowsy, breathing deeply and rapidly, with a fruity smell on his breath. He has lost weight and been drinking and passing urine excessively for weeks. His capillary glucose is far above the measurable range. His blood is acidic, yet the problem began with a hormone that is normally released only when glucose is high. How can too little insulin cause both a sugar excess and an acid excess?

blocks.markdown: **Diabetes mellitus** is a group of disorders in which blood glucose is chronically raised because of absent or ineffective insulin action. Insulin normally promotes glucose uptake into muscle and adipose tissue (through the GLUT4 transporter), glycogen and fat synthesis, and suppresses hepatic glucose output and lipolysis. When insulin action fails, tissues behave as if they were starving even though blood glucose is high: the liver makes glucose by gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, adipose tissue releases fatty acids, and glucagon dominates.

blocks.title: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes
blocks.text: Type 1 diabetes is caused by autoimmune destruction of the pancreatic beta cells, leading to absolute insulin deficiency. Type 2 diabetes is characterised by insulin resistance (target tissues respond poorly to insulin) together with a relative, progressive failure of beta-cell insulin secretion.

rows: Insulin resistance plus relative insulin deficiency
Normal or high early, falling later
Often childhood or young adult, usually lean, rapid onset
Usually adult, often obese; may have acanthosis nigricans (a skin sign of insulin resistance)
Uncommon, because residual insulin restrains lipolysis; hyperosmolar states more likely
Lifestyle and drugs first; insulin may be needed later
blocks.caption: Contrast between type 1 and type 2 diabetes.

blocks.markdown:
**Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): the metabolic chain.** In severe insulin deficiency with excess glucagon:

1. Hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue is no longer restrained, so triacylglycerol is broken down and large amounts of free fatty acids reach the liver.
2. In the liver, fatty acids undergo beta-oxidation at a high rate, generating more acetyl-CoA than the cycle can use. Oxaloacetate is diverted to gluconeogenesis (stimulated by glucagon), so less is available to condense with acetyl-CoA in citrate synthase.
3. Surplus acetyl-CoA is converted to **ketone bodies** (acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate, with a little acetone) through HMG-CoA synthase and HMG-CoA lyase.
4. Acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate are acids; their dissociation consumes bicarbonate and produces a **high anion gap metabolic acidosis**. Acetone is exhaled, causing the fruity breath, and deep rapid (Kussmaul) breathing compensates for the acidosis by blowing off CO2.
5. Glucose above the renal threshold causes an osmotic diuresis, with loss of water and electrolytes and hence dehydration.

blocks.caption: Serum anion gap in mmol/L (potassium omitted by this convention). The reference range varies by laboratory, around 8 to 12 mmol/L.

blocks.title: Why the anion gap rises when ketoacids accumulate
blocks.prompt: A patient has serum sodium 138 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L and bicarbonate 14 mmol/L. Calculate the anion gap and explain what a raised value means.

steps.text: Apply the definition: sodium minus the sum of chloride and bicarbonate.
The gap is 22 mmol/L, above the usual reference range of roughly 8 to 12 mmol/L.

Ketoacid dissociation adds H+ (which consumes HCO3-) and adds an unmeasured anion (acetoacetate or beta-hydroxybutyrate) to plasma. Bicarbonate falls but chloride does not rise, so the difference widens.

blocks.answer: The anion gap is 22 mmol/L, a high anion gap metabolic acidosis consistent with accumulation of unmeasured anions such as ketoacids.

blocks.markdown: **Why type 2 diabetes seldom causes DKA.** In type 2 diabetes there is still enough insulin to suppress lipolysis and hepatic ketogenesis, so ketoacidosis is uncommon. The dominant problem is severe hyperglycaemia causing osmotic diuresis, which in extreme cases leads to a **hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state**. Plasma osmolality can be estimated as 2 x [Na+] + [glucose] + [urea] (all mmol/L).

**Diagnosis: fasting glucose, OGTT and HbA1c.** Glucose is measured after at least 8 hours without food (fasting plasma glucose, FPG). In an **oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)**, glucose is measured 2 hours after a 75 g glucose drink. **HbA1c** is the percentage of haemoglobin that has glucose non-enzymatically and irreversibly attached to it; because red cells live about 120 days, HbA1c reflects the average plasma glucose of roughly the previous 8 to 12 weeks, and is not affected by a single meal. It is expressed as a percentage (NGSP units) or in mmol/mol (IFCC units). Typical criteria (laboratory and guideline thresholds vary): diabetes is diagnosed if FPG is at least 7.0 mmol/L, 2-hour OGTT glucose at least 11.1 mmol/L, or HbA1c at least 6.5 percent (48 mmol/mol); a random glucose at least 11.1 mmol/L with classic symptoms is also diagnostic. In a person without symptoms the abnormal result must be confirmed on a second occasion. Values between normal and the diabetes thresholds (for example FPG about 5.6 or 6.1 to 6.9 mmol/L depending on the guideline, or 2-hour OGTT 7.8 to 11.0 mmol/L) are called prediabetes (impaired fasting glucose or impaired glucose tolerance).

rows: Glucose at one moment after fasting
Ability to clear a glucose load
Average glucose over about 8 to 12 weeks
Unreliable with haemolysis, recent blood loss or transfusion, or some haemoglobin variants
blocks.caption: Common diagnostic tests. Thresholds are widely used but vary by guideline.

blocks.title: Interpreting a pair of results
blocks.prompt: An overweight 50-year-old man with no symptoms has FPG 6.5 mmol/L and HbA1c 44 mmol/mol on the same visit. What do the results mean?

steps.text: Compare FPG with the criterion: 6.5 mmol/L is above normal but below 7.0, so it does not meet the diabetes threshold.
Compare HbA1c with the criterion: 44 mmol/mol is below 48 mmol/mol, so it does not meet the diabetes threshold either.
Both are in the intermediate range, consistent with prediabetes (raised risk of diabetes). Lifestyle advice and re-testing are appropriate.

blocks.answer: Prediabetes: neither FPG nor HbA1c reaches the diabetes threshold, but both are above normal.

items: Type 1: absolute insulin deficiency; type 2: insulin resistance with relative deficiency.
DKA arises from insulin deficiency plus glucagon excess: lipolysis, fatty acid oxidation, ketogenesis, high anion gap acidosis and osmotic diuresis.
Ketone bodies are acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetone.
HbA1c shows long-term glycaemia; fasting glucose shows the glucose level at one time.

blocks.title: Unreliable HbA1c
blocks.text: Anything that shortens red cell life (haemolysis, bleeding) lowers HbA1c and may hide diabetes; interpret HbA1c cautiously in anaemia and haemoglobin variants, and use plasma glucose instead.

points: Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune insulin deficiency; type 2 is insulin resistance with relative deficiency.
DKA results from unrestrained lipolysis and ketogenesis in the absence of insulin, producing a high anion gap metabolic acidosis with dehydration.
Diabetes is diagnosed from FPG, 2-hour OGTT glucose or HbA1c against standard thresholds, with confirmation when asymptomatic.
HbA1c reflects glycaemia over 8 to 12 weeks but is unreliable when red cell lifespan is altered.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes omits her insulin for two days during a vomiting illness and presents with deep breathing and abdominal pain. What is the primary biochemical driver of her ketoacidosis?

options.text: Insulin deficiency with unrestrained lipolysis and hepatic ketone body production
Excess insulin driving glucose into cells and depleting blood glucose
Failure of the kidney to excrete ketone bodies as the primary defect
Excess lactate production by muscle during hyperventilation

questions.correctOptionText: Insulin deficiency with unrestrained lipolysis and hepatic ketone body production

distractorRationale.a: Correct: without insulin, adipose lipolysis releases fatty acids that the liver converts to ketone bodies.
distractorRationale.b: Insulin is lacking, not in excess.
distractorRationale.c: Ketone bodies accumulate because they are overproduced, not because of a primary renal defect.
distractorRationale.d: The deep breathing is a compensation for the acidosis, not its cause.

questions.explanation: Absence of insulin releases the brake on hormone-sensitive lipase, so fatty acids flood the liver and are oxidised to acetyl-CoA and converted to ketone bodies. These dissociate to produce acid. The breathing is a compensatory response.

questions.stem: In the liver during diabetic ketoacidosis, why is surplus acetyl-CoA diverted into ketone bodies rather than being fully oxidised in the citric acid cycle?

options.text: Beta-oxidation generates more acetyl-CoA than the cycle can accept, and oxaloacetate is diverted to gluconeogenesis
Insulin directly activates HMG-CoA synthase
The cycle enzymes are destroyed by the acidosis
Acetyl-CoA cannot enter mitochondria in the liver

questions.correctOptionText: Beta-oxidation generates more acetyl-CoA than the cycle can accept, and oxaloacetate is diverted to gluconeogenesis

distractorRationale.a: Correct: oxaloacetate is needed for citrate synthase and is limited when used for glucose synthesis.
distractorRationale.b: Insulin is deficient in DKA and, if anything, suppresses ketogenesis.
distractorRationale.c: The cycle enzymes are not destroyed; flux is limited by oxaloacetate and NADH.
distractorRationale.d: Acetyl-CoA from beta-oxidation is formed inside mitochondria.

questions.explanation: High fatty acid oxidation produces a large acetyl-CoA load. Glucagon-driven gluconeogenesis draws off oxaloacetate, so citrate synthase is limited and acetyl-CoA condenses to acetoacetyl-CoA and then HMG-CoA, forming ketone bodies.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old obese man has acanthosis nigricans in his axillae, a fasting glucose of 8.2 mmol/L and a raised fasting insulin level. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: Type 2 diabetes with insulin resistance and compensatory hyperinsulinaemia
Type 1 diabetes with absolute insulin deficiency
Insulin deficiency due to autoimmune destruction of beta cells
Normal physiology, because fasting insulin is raised

questions.correctOptionText: Type 2 diabetes with insulin resistance and compensatory hyperinsulinaemia

distractorRationale.a: Correct: raised insulin with raised glucose indicates tissues are resistant to insulin.
distractorRationale.b: In type 1 diabetes insulin is very low or absent.
distractorRationale.c: Autoimmune beta-cell loss would lower, not raise, insulin.
distractorRationale.d: A fasting glucose of 8.2 mmol/L is above the diabetes threshold of 7.0.

questions.explanation: Raised insulin alongside raised glucose means the tissues are resistant to insulin's action; the beta cells compensate initially and later fail. Acanthosis nigricans is a skin marker of insulin resistance. In type 1 disease insulin would be low or absent.

questions.stem: A woman with a chronic haemolytic anaemia has a fasting plasma glucose of 9.2 mmol/L on two mornings but an HbA1c of 4.8 percent. Which is the best explanation for the low HbA1c?

options.text: Shortened red cell survival leaves less time for glycation, so HbA1c underestimates average glucose
HbA1c measures glucose at the time of the test only
HbA1c is raised by haemolysis, so the true value is even lower
The fasting glucose must be a laboratory error because HbA1c is always more accurate

questions.correctOptionText: Shortened red cell survival leaves less time for glycation, so HbA1c underestimates average glucose

distractorRationale.a: Correct: younger red cells have had less exposure to glucose.
distractorRationale.b: HbA1c reflects the past 8 to 12 weeks, not a single moment.
distractorRationale.d: Two consistent fasting values of 9.2 mmol/L are reliable and exceed 7.0.

questions.explanation: Glycation is cumulative over the life of the red cell. If red cells are destroyed early, the haemoglobin has less time to become glycated, so HbA1c falls. Two fasting glucose values above 7.0 mmol/L diagnose diabetes regardless of this unreliable HbA1c.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has a fasting plasma glucose of 6.3 mmol/L and a 2-hour OGTT glucose of 9.0 mmol/L. Using the criteria in this unit, how should the result be classified?

options.text: Prediabetes, because neither value reaches the diabetes threshold
Diabetes mellitus, because fasting glucose is above 5.5 mmol/L
Normal, because the 2-hour value is below 11.1 mmol/L
Type 1 diabetes, because the 2-hour value is above 7.8 mmol/L

questions.correctOptionText: Prediabetes, because neither value reaches the diabetes threshold

distractorRationale.a: Correct: FPG is below 7.0 and the 2-hour value of 9.0 lies in the 7.8 to 11.0 range.
distractorRationale.b: The diabetes threshold for FPG is 7.0 mmol/L, not 5.5.
distractorRationale.c: Both values are above normal, so the result is not normal.
distractorRationale.d: OGTT does not classify type; and 9.0 is below the diabetes threshold.

questions.explanation: Fasting glucose of 6.3 is in the impaired fasting range (below 7.0), and a 2-hour OGTT value of 9.0 is in the impaired glucose tolerance range (7.8 to 11.0). Neither reaches the diabetes threshold, so this is prediabetes, which carries a raised risk of progression.

questions.stem: True or false: diabetic ketoacidosis is less common in type 2 than in type 1 diabetes because residual insulin in type 2 diabetes restrains lipolysis.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Type 2 diabetes involves insulin resistance with some remaining insulin secretion, which is enough to restrain adipose lipolysis and ketone production. Type 1 diabetes has absolute insulin deficiency, so DKA is much more likely.

questions.stem: A patient with suspected diabetic ketoacidosis has serum sodium 136 mmol/L, chloride 96 mmol/L and bicarbonate 8 mmol/L. Calculate the anion gap (omit potassium) in mmol/L.
questions.explanation: Anion gap = sodium - (chloride + bicarbonate) = 136 - (96 + 8) = 136 - 104 = 32 mmol/L. This is far above the usual range of about 8 to 12 mmol/L, consistent with accumulation of unmeasured ketoacid anions.

questions.stem: A patient with severe uncontrolled hyperglycaemia has serum sodium 132 mmol/L, glucose 34 mmol/L and urea 12 mmol/L. Estimate the plasma osmolality in mOsm/kg using 2 x [Na+] + [glucose] + [urea], with all concentrations in mmol/L.
questions.explanation: Twice the sodium accounts for sodium plus its accompanying anions: 2 x 132 = 264. Adding glucose (34) and urea (12) gives 264 + 34 + 12 = 310 mOsm/kg. Glucose contributes 34 of this, which is why very high glucose causes osmotic diuresis and dehydration.

questions.stem: Explain the sequence of metabolic events that links absolute insulin deficiency to ketoacidosis, naming the organs and key pathways, and say why hyperglycaemia also causes dehydration.
markingGuide: Insulin deficiency and glucagon excess: hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue is unrestrained, releasing free fatty acids
Liver takes up fatty acids, enhanced beta-oxidation produces excess acetyl-CoA
Oxaloacetate is diverted to gluconeogenesis, limiting citrate synthase so acetyl-CoA goes to ketone body synthesis (acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetone)
Ketoacids dissociate, consuming bicarbonate: high anion gap metabolic acidosis; Kussmaul breathing compensates
Hyperglycaemia exceeds the renal threshold, causing osmotic diuresis with loss of water and electrolytes
Peripheral tissues cannot take up glucose without insulin, and the liver adds more through gluconeogenesis
questions.explanation: Without insulin, fat is mobilised and the liver converts the resulting acetyl-CoA into ketone bodies, whose acidity lowers bicarbonate and pH. At the same time, glucose cannot be used and rises, causing osmotic diuresis and dehydration.

questions.stem: Contrast type 1 and type 2 diabetes in terms of insulin deficiency and insulin resistance, and explain why ketoacidosis is more typical of type 1 diabetes.
markingGuide: Type 1: autoimmune destruction of beta cells, absolute insulin deficiency, low or absent C-peptide, usually lean and younger
Type 2: insulin resistance in muscle, liver and adipose tissue with relative insulin deficiency, often obese, insulin initially raised
Type 1 patients cannot suppress lipolysis and ketogenesis without exogenous insulin, so they develop DKA
In type 2, residual insulin restrains lipolysis; severe hyperglycaemia and hyperosmolar state are more typical
Treatment: type 1 always needs insulin; type 2 often begins with lifestyle and oral drugs
questions.explanation: The difference is the amount of insulin available: none in type 1, but plentiful and ineffective, then eventually insufficient, in type 2. Because some insulin remains in type 2, lipolysis and ketogenesis are restrained, which is why DKA is typical of type 1.
